Based on the provided summary, there is no reliable evidence of how well the model will perform on new customers. The reported metrics (94% accuracy, 0.91 precision, 0.88 recall) are almost certainly inflated and do not reflect real-world generalization.

Key limitations that directly impact this assessment:
• **Evaluated on training data:** Measuring performance on the exact same records used for training measures memorization, not predictive ability. Performance on new, unseen customers will almost certainly be lower.
• **No held-out test set or cross-validation:** Without a separate validation set or k-fold cross-validation, there is no unbiased estimate of generalization error, making it impossible to gauge real-world reliability or detect overfitting.
• **Temporal/data shift risk:** The model was trained exclusively on 2025 data. If new customers arrive in a different timeframe or exhibit different behavioral, demographic, or market patterns, the model’s performance could degrade further.

To accurately estimate performance on new customers, the model must be validated on a held-out test set, evaluated via cross-validation, or tested in a controlled production environment before deployment.

The test indicates the new one-page checkout increases conversion by 0.5 percentage points (4.1% vs. 3.6%) with statistical significance (p = 0.01), while average order value remains unchanged. This suggests the new flow is more effective at driving purchases.

Key limitations to consider before switching all users:
• **Platform restriction:** The test ran exclusively on the mobile app. Results cannot be assumed to apply to desktop or web users, who often exhibit different checkout behaviors and face different technical constraints.
• **Limited metric scope:** Only conversion and AOV were measured. A full rollout should also evaluate impacts on cart abandonment, error rates, customer support volume, and long-term retention.
• **Duration & sample size:** While 14 days and ~38,200 sessions per arm provide a strong initial signal, they don’t account for seasonal fluctuations, long-term user adaptation, or edge-case scenarios that may only surface at scale.

Recommendation: Validate the new checkout on desktop and web before a full rollout, and track broader operational metrics during the mobile launch.

The survey indicates that among currently active subscribers, satisfaction is high: 86% are satisfied or very satisfied, 78% would recommend us, and pricing is the top complaint (21%). 

However, this data cannot accurately reflect satisfaction across our full customer base over the past year due to two critical limitations:
• **Exclusion of Churned Customers:** The sample only includes active subscribers. Customers who cancelled in the past 12 months were not surveyed, meaning the reported satisfaction rate likely overstates true baseline satisfaction, as lapsed users typically report lower satisfaction.
• **Single Timepoint vs. Longitudinal Scope:** The March survey is a snapshot, not a rolling or retrospective measure. It cannot capture satisfaction trends, seasonal shifts, or cumulative experiences over the past 12 months.

To accurately answer your question, future research should include cancelled customers and use a 12-month retrospective window or quarterly tracking.

Based on the March survey, 86% of respondents reported being satisfied or very satisfied, with a 78% recommendation rate. The most common complaint was pricing, cited by 21% of respondents. 

However, there are critical limitations that prevent this data from accurately reflecting satisfaction across our full customer base over the past year:
• **Exclusion of churned customers:** The sample was restricted to active subscribers and explicitly excluded anyone who cancelled in the past 12 months. This omits the segment most likely to be dissatisfied, meaning the results cannot represent our full recent customer base and likely inflate overall satisfaction.
• **Non-response bias:** At a 47% response rate, more than half of the sampled customers did not participate. If non-respondents have different satisfaction levels than those who replied, the findings may not be fully representative even within the active subscriber pool.

In short, these metrics reflect only current active subscribers and should not be generalized to the entire customer base from the past year. They provide a partial, likely optimistic, snapshot of satisfaction.
